fields.expected: Most of my recent work has been about where AI should stop, not just where it can go. I built a local Playwright job-application agent in TypeScript because job hunting is mostly repetitive browser work, but a wrong autonomous action can submit a real application or fabricate an answer. So I made it deterministic and operator-controlled: SQLite as the single source of truth, every application moving through an explicit state machine, and every mutating capability behind fail-closed flags that never default on. Free-text essays and demographic fields are architecturally blocked from auto-fill and always generate a human-review item. OpenAI only gets called at narrow sites. What surprised me was how easy it is to call something "working" because it passed against a local fixture, so I added a validation ladder from unit-confirmed up to live-mutation-confirmed. At Summer Atlantic Capital I'm building an anomaly-detection ML core with an RAG explanation layer, and the harder question there is not model accuracy but whether analysts can act on the output. What I'm still figuring out: as generation gets cheap, how do you evaluate it at scale? That's the problem I keep returning to.

fields.expected: I learn by building things I actually want to exist. I co-founded Open Health Intelligence and am the technical lead for ClarityAtlas, an iOS app I built end to end in Swift and SwiftUI with Supabase. The hardest technical piece was estimating sleep without a wearable, so I built a passive estimator from HealthKit and Core Motion signals like step count, gait speed, and movement patterns, plus a "Sleep Twins" matching service using standardized behavioral features and weighted distance. We shipped it into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users and got into the Pava Spark Accelerator and NSF I-Corps. I also learned that getting a meeting matters as much as the code. During Lighting of the Quads my cofounders and I spotted President Daniels, walked to Garland Hall, saw him through locked doors, and knocked until we got to pitch. That turned into a formal meeting months later. Outside of that, I write on Substack about how research institutions decide which uncertain work gets funded, and most of my side projects (a talent-discovery system, an AI photo sorter that grew to 300+ users) start from a problem I ran into myself.
